chapter.title: Across the pool, and staying safe

cards.body: Every chapter so far added one movement on top of the bed. Today you lie on it and let it carry you the whole way. Picture the far wall, 12 metres off, and your hand reaching it. **Nothing between here and there is new**: push, glide, kick, arms, breath. The only new skill is knowing what to do when it wobbles.
cards.simpler: Each chapter so far added one small move. Today you put them all together and let the water carry you across. Picture the far wall, 12 metres away, and your hand touching it. **Nothing between here and there is new**: push off, glide, kick, arms, breathe. The only new thing you learn today is what to do if it goes wobbly.

cards.prompt: Halfway across the width, Ana's arms turn to lead and her breathing goes ragged. What fixes it fastest?

options.text: Kick harder and get to the wall before the air runs out.
Roll onto her back, float, and breathe until it passes.
Lift her head high and paddle hard with both arms.

whyNot.a: That's sprinting, not resting: harder work burns the air faster, and the wall doesn't come closer because you hurry.
whyNot.c: That's the panic shape, not the rest shape: a high head makes the hips sink, and sinking hips make you work harder still.

cards.reteach: Tired in the water is not an emergency. It's a signal to stop working. On your back your face is in the air, and a full chest of air holds you up with no effort at all. Rest first, then decide.

cards.title: Joining it up
cards.body:
Push off the wall into your long glide. Let it slow, then start the small kick from chapter 5. When the kick settles, add the arms: one reaches, one pulls, face down, breathing out slowly through your nose.

**Breathe when you need to, not when you're desperate.** Lift your head forward, take a breath, face back in, carry on. Side breathing comes later. For now a lifted head every 3 or 4 strokes is fine.

Go slow. Slow swimming floats. Fast swimming, for a new swimmer, mostly splashes.
cards.simpler:
Push off the wall and glide. When the glide slows, start the kick from chapter 5. When the kick settles, add the arms: one reaches forward, one pulls back. Face down, breathing out through your nose.

**Breathe when you need to, not when you're desperate.** Lift your head forward, breathe in, face back in, carry on. Side breathing comes later. A lifted head every 3 or 4 strokes is fine.

Slow swimming floats. Fast swimming mostly splashes.

cards.title: Sam's boring crossing
cards.body: Sam pushes off, glides, kicks, and gets 4 strokes in before lifting to breathe. 3 more strokes, then at stroke 7 the arms go heavy. Sam rolls over onto the back float, looks at the ceiling lights for about 10 seconds, breathes, rolls back, and takes 4 more strokes to the wall. **The crossing took 40 seconds instead of 20, and the lifeguard never looked up.** That is the goal. Boring is what safe looks like.
cards.simpler: Sam pushes off, glides, kicks, and takes 4 strokes before lifting up to breathe. 3 more strokes. At stroke 7 the arms feel heavy. So Sam rolls over onto the back float, looks up at the ceiling lights for about 10 seconds, breathes, rolls back, and takes 4 more strokes to reach the wall. **The crossing took 40 seconds instead of 20, and the lifeguard never looked up.** That is the goal. Boring is what safe looks like.

cards.prompt: Three friends at the pool. Who has set things up so that the rest on your back always works?

options.text: Dev swims alone at 6am in the deep end because it's quiet.
Maya swims widths in the chest-deep part, her sister on the side, and lies back whenever she's puffed.
Leo swims widths where he can stand, but holds his breath the whole way and sprints to the wall.

whyNot.a: That's quiet confused with safe: alone and deep means no one to notice and no floor to find if the float goes badly.
whyNot.c: That's the right place with chapter 2 undone: a held breath and a sprint are how you arrive gasping. Breathe out, go slow.

cards.reteach: The back float is your rest button. The habits are what keep you where the button works: water you can stand in, a person who can see you, a slow pace with the breath going out. Maya has all three.

cards.title: The 4 habits
cards.body:
Every habit here is the same sentence: **stay where the water can hold you up and someone can see you.**

One: swim where you can stand, until the deep-end chapters later. Two: swim with someone, or where a lifeguard can see you. A quiet empty pool is not a bonus. Three: never jump into water you don't know the depth of. Read the markings, get in feet first by the ladder. Four: when you're tired, roll onto your back and rest. Not later. Now.

Say the four out loud once on the way home.
cards.simpler:
All four habits say one thing: **stay where the water can hold you up and someone can see you.**

One: swim where you can stand, for now. Two: swim with a friend, or where a lifeguard can see you. Three: never jump in if you don't know the depth. Read the markings, get in feet first by the ladder. Four: when tired, roll onto your back and rest. Not later. Now.

Say all four out loud going home.

cards.body: Tom crosses once, feels brilliant, and turns straight round for the return with no rest. Halfway back the breath goes, the head comes up, the hips drop, and the arms start thrashing. The spot-it signal is **your head rising and your breathing getting loud**. That is the cue to stop and lie back, not the cue to swim harder.
cards.simpler: Tom crosses once, feels great, and turns straight round to swim back with no rest. Halfway back the breath runs out. The head comes up, the hips sink, and the arms start thrashing. The warning sign to watch for is **your head rising and your breathing getting loud**. That is your cue to stop and lie back on the water, not your cue to swim harder.

cards.prompt: Why does lying on your back work as a rest, when front crawl doesn't?

options.text: Because your back floats better than your front.
Because your face is out of the water, so you can breathe with no effort, and a lungful of air keeps your chest up.
Because kicking on your back is faster, so you reach the wall sooner.

whyNot.a: That's the shape confused with the air: your body floats the same either way, as in chapter 3. The difference is where your mouth is.
whyNot.c: That's speed, not rest. A rest is when you stop moving and the bed holds you anyway.

cards.reteach: Front crawl needs your face in the water, so breathing takes work. On your back, breathing is free. Fill your lungs and the water does the holding, which is the whole picture of this handbook.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Push off, kick, add the arms, breathe out, lift to breathe in, and the width takes care of itself. **If anything goes wrong, roll onto your back**: the water holds you up, and that was the whole handbook.
cards.simpler: Push off, kick, add the arms, breathe out, lift your head to breathe in, and the width of the pool takes care of itself. **If anything goes wrong, roll onto your back.** The water holds you up while you rest, like lying on a mattress. That one move is what the whole handbook has been building to.

cards.body: Next swim, do one width. On the second, roll onto your back halfway on purpose, float 10 seconds, roll back and finish. Practise the rest when you don't need it, so it's there when you do.
cards.simpler: Next time you swim, do one width of the pool. On the second width, roll onto your back halfway across on purpose. Float for 10 seconds, roll back over, and finish the width. **Practise the rest when you don't need it**, so it is there, ready, on the day you do.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now swim a slow front crawl across the pool, roll onto your back to rest when you need to, and name the 4 habits that keep you safe every swim.
